title: Electro-Optical Metalens for Near-Surface Cooling of a Levitated Particle
authors: Pedro Rosso Gomez, Bruno Melo, Adeel Afridi, Mohamed Sabry Mohamed, Nadine Meyer, Romain Quidant
abstract: Advanced levitation optomechanics in the quantum regime requires sophisticated quantumengineered protocols operating at shorter length and time scales, demanding an increasing control over both optical and electrical potentials. Integrated chip-scale platforms offer a natural route toward such control. Here, we demonstrate optical levitation in vacuum using a miniaturized hybrid electro-optical metalens. Motion control is achieved using a high numerical aperture metalens combined with electrical active feedback using planar electrodes, enabling cooling to low phonon occupations. Reheating measurements enable us to rule out any significant influence from electric field noise; an encouraging result for the future development of on-chip levitation platforms operating close to surfaces. This compact integrated platform facilitates the precise manipulation and control of levitated nanoparticles while laying the ground toward exploiting the full capacity of metaoptics to engineer complex optical potentials, marking a significant step forward in technologies for quantum levitation optomechanics.
summary: This paper presents an integrated chip-scale platform using a metalens for optical levitation and active electrical feedback for motion control of a nanoparticle. The authors successfully cooled the particle's motion to low phonon occupations in vacuum. This work marks a significant step toward realizing complex, controllable quantum levitation systems on a chip.
main_problem: The challenge is achieving advanced levitation optomechanics in the quantum regime, requiring precise control over both optical and electrical potentials at short length and time scales.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated optical levitation and motion control down to low phonon occupation using a compact, integrated electro-optical metalens platform.
method: They combined a high numerical aperture metalens for optical trapping with active electrical feedback applied via planar electrodes to damp the particle's center-of-mass motion.
model_or_system: The system involves a charged nanoparticle levitated in vacuum above a hybrid electro-optical metalens chip. The trapping potential is engineered optically, and the motion control is achieved by applying feedback forces derived from planar electrodes.
key_observables: Low phonon occupations ($ ar{n}_{min,j}$), mechanical eigenfrequencies ($\Omega_j$), and the time evolution of phonon occupation ($ ar{n}_j(t)$) after feedback is removed.
important_parameters: Trapping power ($P_t$), particle radius ($R$), planar electrode voltages ($V_{\pm x}, V_{f,b z}$), and ambient pressure ($p_{gas}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the potential can be reconstructed via the Gibbs probability density function, and they specifically tested for and ruled out significant electrical field noise as a heating source.
figures_summary: Figure 1 details the metalens structure and intensity profiles. Figure 2 shows the experimental setup and the dependence of mechanical eigenfrequencies on optical power. Figure 3 and 4 illustrate the particle's power spectral density and the time decay of phonon occupation, respectively.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need for advanced control in quantum optomechanics, detailing the metalens design and its application for trapping, demonstrating active cooling via electrical feedback, and finally analyzing heating sources by measuring phonon decay rates.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it pushes the boundaries of integrated quantum optomechanics by combining metaoptics for complex potential engineering with active electrical feedback for quantum cooling, directly addressing open quantum system control.
